items.question:
A communications manager at an energy company uses Claude to produce a one-page summary of a 60-page sustainability report for a stakeholder briefing. The source report states that the company reduced scope 2 emissions by 18% year-on-year. Claude's summary states the reduction was 'approximately 20%.' The communications manager reviews the summary for tone and format before sending it.

What type of error is present, and what verification step would have caught it?

options.A: A commission error; it would have been caught by comparing the specific percentage in the summary against the corresponding figure in the source report.
options.B: An omission error; it would have been caught by checking that all key metrics from the source report appear in the summary.
options.C: A calibration error; it would have been caught by asking Claude to express the percentage with greater precision in the output.
options.D: A staleness error; it would have been caught by providing Claude with the most recent version of the sustainability report as context.

items.question:
A healthcare data analyst at a hospital network uses Claude to summarise patient satisfaction survey results from 3,200 responses. The source data shows that satisfaction with discharge instructions was the lowest-rated category at 52%. Claude's summary highlights the top four satisfaction categories but does not mention discharge instruction satisfaction at all.

Why is this omission particularly significant in a healthcare context?

options.A: Because the omission means Claude produced a commission error by fabricating the top four categories.
options.B: Because a reviewer reading only the summary would not know that the lowest-scoring category exists, potentially directing improvement resources away from the area most needing attention.
options.C: Because discharge instruction satisfaction data is not reliably extracted from survey data by AI models and should always be verified separately.
options.D: Because patient satisfaction surveys are regulated documents and omissions in summaries constitute a compliance violation requiring immediate reporting.

items.question:
A compliance analyst at a financial services firm uses Claude to convert a 25-page internal policy document into a structured checklist of 40 compliance actions. After distribution, two team members independently notice that checklist item 17 reads 'obtain approval from the risk committee within 5 business days' but the source policy states 'obtain approval from the chief risk officer within 3 business days.' Two details are wrong simultaneously.

Which TWO statements accurately characterise this error? (Choose TWO)

options.A: This is a commission error because the checklist contains content ('risk committee,' '5 business days') that is not present in the source policy.
options.B: This error creates a compliance risk because team members following the checklist may seek the wrong approval from the wrong party within the wrong timeframe.
options.C: This is an omission error because the correct approval details present in the source policy are absent from the checklist item.
options.D: The error would have been caught by comparing the number of checklist items against the number of distinct actions in the source policy.
options.E: Claude's training data likely contains a similar policy that used 'risk committee' and '5 business days,' causing it to blend two documents.

items.question:
A tax analyst at a professional services firm uses Claude to extract effective tax rate (ETR) figures and deferred tax asset balances from the footnotes of 22 client annual reports. The extractions will feed a benchmarking model comparing clients against their industry peers. Each annual report has a different footnote structure and uses varying terminology for the same concepts.

Which verification risk is MOST elevated in this specific scenario compared to a standardised template-based extraction?

options.A: Claude may refuse to extract tax data from annual reports due to the sensitive financial nature of the content.
options.B: Inconsistent terminology and varying footnote structures increase the risk that Claude maps a figure to the wrong concept or field, producing plausible values that are structurally correct but semantically wrong.
options.C: Claude's context window may be exceeded by annual reports longer than 100 pages, causing it to truncate and miss footnote data silently.
options.D: Without a standardised template, Claude cannot generate a JSON-formatted output, requiring the analyst to convert the output to a structured format manually.

items.question:
An HR analyst at a manufacturing company uses Claude to convert 150 employee job titles from the company's legacy system format (e.g., 'ENGR-SR-MECH-3') into plain-language job titles (e.g., 'Senior Mechanical Engineer - Grade 3') for a new HR platform. She reviews the output by scanning the plain-language titles for obvious anomalies.

Which additional verification step would MOST improve confidence in the accuracy of the transformation?

options.A: Ask Claude to generate a confidence score for each transformed title, and manually review any title scored below 80% confidence.
options.B: Submit the output to the HR platform and verify that the system accepts all 150 titles without errors during import.
options.C: Randomly select 15-20 transformed titles and trace each one back to its source code to confirm the mapping is correct.
options.D: Distribute the plain-language titles to department heads and ask them to flag any title that does not match their team's job level structure.

items.question:
An operations analyst at a telecoms company uses Claude to generate a monthly KPI summary from a data dump of the company's operational database. The summary will be presented to the executive team. Before finalising the summary, the analyst wants to verify the key figures.

What is the MOST reliable verification approach for the KPI figures?

options.A: Ask Claude to re-run the analysis and compare the two outputs to confirm the figures are consistent before presenting them.
options.B: Compare the KPI figures in Claude's summary against the same KPIs pulled directly from the operational database system of record for the reporting period.
options.C: Forward the draft summary to a colleague and ask them to read it for reasonableness based on their operational experience.
options.D: Check that the KPI figures in the summary fall within the historical range for each metric based on prior monthly reports.

items.question:
A quality assurance lead at a pharma company uses Claude to generate batch release summaries from 200-page batch records. The summaries will be reviewed by the QA team before batch release decisions are made. A process improvement manager suggests that the summaries can bypass QA review once Claude achieves a 99% accuracy rate in testing, since the rate effectively means fewer errors than human review.

Which response BEST addresses this suggestion from a verification governance perspective?

options.A: Accept the proposal, since a 99% accuracy rate on tested batches statistically demonstrates that Claude outperforms human review and the quality risk is negligible.
options.B: Accept the proposal only for standard batches, with QA review retained for non-standard batches and any batch where deviations were recorded during production.
options.C: Reject the proposal; for regulated batch release decisions, a qualified QA professional must remain in the verification loop regardless of AI accuracy rates in testing.
options.D: Accept the proposal provisionally and set an alert for any output where Claude's internal confidence falls below a defined threshold requiring human review.

items.question:
An investment analyst at an asset management firm is designing a workflow in which Claude synthesises daily news and company announcements into a morning briefing for portfolio managers. The briefing is used to inform intraday trading decisions. She is debating whether to verify the briefing content before it is distributed each morning or after.

Which TWO considerations MOST strongly argue for pre-distribution verification of the briefing? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Pre-distribution verification ensures the briefing meets the firm's house style guide before it reaches portfolio managers.
options.B: Intraday trading decisions made on the basis of a factually incorrect briefing can result in financial losses that cannot be reversed once a trade is executed.
options.C: Claude's summarisation of company announcements may omit material non-public information that pre-distribution review would identify.
options.D: An incorrect or materially misleading briefing distributed to portfolio managers could constitute a breach of the firm's fiduciary duty to clients.
options.E: Post-distribution review is sufficient because portfolio managers have access to source news feeds and can independently verify claims of interest.

items.question:
A project manager at a construction company uses Claude to generate 30 progress reports from site logs each month. The reports are shared with clients and used to approve payment milestones. The company's contract with the client requires that all progress reports be reviewed and certified by a qualified site engineer before release.

Which practice BEST ensures the documentation requirement is met for each report?

options.A: Have the project manager sign each report before sending, confirming that the content reflects their understanding of the project status.
options.B: Store the AI-generated draft alongside the final report in the project management system, which shows the version history as implicit evidence of review.
options.C: Require the qualified site engineer to sign a review certificate for each report, recording the review date, report version reviewed, and certification outcome.
options.D: Include a footer in each report stating 'Reviewed by site engineering team' to satisfy the client contract requirement.

items.question:
A customer success manager at a SaaS company uses Claude to generate personalised renewal discussion summaries for 60 customer accounts each quarter. The summaries draw on account health data and past support interactions. She sends them directly to account executives 48 hours before renewal calls.

Which verification approach is MOST appropriate before she distributes the summaries?

options.A: Send all 60 summaries to account executives without review, since they know their accounts and will catch any inaccuracies during the renewal call.
options.B: Have a sales leader review all 60 summaries to ensure they align with the company's renewal messaging strategy.
options.C: Review a random sample of 8-10 summaries by spot-checking key account health data against the source system before distributing the full set.
options.D: Ask Claude to review all 60 summaries for internal consistency before sending them to account executives.

items.question:
A market researcher at a retail company uses Claude to generate 250 structured competitor product profiles from web data each month. The profiles feed a pricing model that adjusts the company's own product prices daily. Two profiles contain incorrect pricing data that inflates a competitor's price, causing the model to raise the company's prices unnecessarily for three days.

What change to the verification workflow would BEST prevent this type of error going forward?

options.A: Increase the sample rate for pricing data fields specifically, and validate those fields against a second independent source before the profiles enter the pricing model.
options.B: Switch to manual research for all 250 profiles, since AI-generated pricing data is inherently unreliable for pricing model inputs.
options.C: Ask Claude to generate confidence scores for each profile and exclude any profile where confidence falls below a defined threshold.
options.D: Require that the pricing model incorporate a human approval step before any price adjustment exceeds 5% of the current price.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs specialist at a medtech company uses Claude to draft a 510(k) submission section that describes clinical performance data from three clinical evaluation reports (CERs), totalling 420 pages. The draft cites 34 specific performance figures. The specialist submits the draft to a senior regulatory manager for review. The manager returns it with 6 corrections to specific figures.

The specialist wants to redesign the verification workflow to prevent similar corrections in future submissions. Which approach is MOST likely to reduce figure errors to near-zero for this type of submission?

options.A: Instruct Claude to include a source citation (report name, page, and table number) for each performance figure in the draft, then verify each citation resolves to the stated figure.
options.B: Ask Claude to regenerate the draft and count whether the number of figures in the regenerated version differs from the original, using any discrepancy as a flag for manual review.
options.C: Use a plausibility check table: compile the expected ranges for each performance metric based on industry benchmarks and flag any figure that falls outside the range.
options.D: Increase the number of review cycles before submission, requiring two additional internal reviewers to read the full draft before the regulatory manager sees it.

items.question:
A communications director at a regional healthcare provider uses Claude to condense a 100-page patient experience report into a 2-page board summary. The source report contains a section stating that emergency department (ED) wait time satisfaction declined 14 percentage points year-on-year. Claude's summary describes ED satisfaction as 'somewhat lower than the prior year.' The board summary is presented at the quarterly board meeting without the communications director verifying it against the source.

Which TWO aspects of this specific summary error are MOST significant from a governance perspective? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The summary transformed a specific, material quantitative finding (a 14 percentage point decline) into a vague qualitative description, which understates the severity of the finding.
options.B: The communications director should have used a higher model tier to ensure the quantitative figure was preserved accurately in the summary.
options.C: The board received a materially misleading picture of ED performance, which may affect the quality and urgency of the board's response to a significant patient experience decline.
options.D: The use of AI to generate board summaries requires explicit disclosure to the board at every meeting where AI-assisted content is presented.
options.E: Claude's tendency to soften negative findings is a known reliability limitation that makes it unsuitable for patient experience reporting.

items.question:
A grant writer at a non-profit uses Claude to summarise a successful funding proposal — including objectives, activities, and expected outcomes — into a 1-page case study for donor communications. The original 35-page proposal includes a section on project risks and mitigation strategies. The 1-page case study does not mention risks at all.

A major donor asks whether there is a risk section in the full proposal. The grant writer is surprised — she had not noticed its absence from the case study.

What does this scenario illustrate about omission errors in summarisation?

options.A: It illustrates that Claude hallucinated the positive content in the case study and should have focused on risks instead.
options.B: It illustrates that Claude's training data does not include enough examples of risk sections in grant proposals, leading to systematic omission.
options.C: It illustrates that omission errors can go unnoticed by the person who produced the summary if they did not verify it against the source document.
options.D: It illustrates that case studies should not be generated by AI because donors will ask questions the AI cannot anticipate.

items.question:
A brand manager at a consumer goods company uses Claude to rewrite product specification sheets for 80 products to comply with a new EU labelling format. For one product, the source specification shows an allergen warning for 'contains soy.' Claude's rewritten sheet reads 'may contain traces of soy.' The brand manager reviews the sheets for format compliance before distribution to retailers.

What type of error is this, and why is it particularly significant in this context?

options.A: An omission error, because the 'contains soy' warning was removed from the specification and the 'may contain traces' statement does not appear in the source document.
options.B: A commission error, because Claude changed the legal declaration ('contains soy') to a precautionary advisory ('may contain traces of soy'), which has a different regulatory meaning and reduces the strength of the allergen warning.
options.C: A staleness error, because Claude's training data may not include the most recent EU allergen labelling regulations, leading it to apply outdated standards.
options.D: A calibration error, because Claude expressed inappropriate uncertainty about the presence of soy by adding 'traces of' to an otherwise accurate statement.

items.question:
A claims examiner at a workers compensation insurance carrier uses Claude to extract 8 specific data fields from 300 medical reports per week: diagnosis codes, treatment dates, provider NPI numbers, and maximum medical improvement (MMI) dates. A carrier audit reveals that 4% of extracted diagnosis codes contain a character transposition (e.g., M54.5 extracted as M45.5), resulting in incorrect claim classifications.

Which combination of verification controls would MOST effectively reduce the transposition error rate for diagnosis codes specifically?

options.A: Add a cross-reference check: after extraction, validate each extracted diagnosis code against the ICD code registry to confirm the code exists as a valid code.
options.B: Add a plausibility check: flag any extracted diagnosis code that is not among the 20 most common workers compensation diagnosis codes for review.
options.C: Combine a code-validity check against the ICD registry with a spot-check of 15-20% of codes by tracing them back to the exact location in the source medical report.
options.D: Re-run the extraction for all 300 reports weekly and flag any code that differs between the two runs as requiring manual review.

items.question:
A finance analyst at a global manufacturing company uses Claude to convert 400 local-currency financial statements from 12 subsidiaries into a consolidated USD reporting format. The conversion requires applying different exchange rates for each subsidiary (rates are provided in a reference table pasted into the prompt). She reviews the output by checking that all 12 subsidiaries are represented and that total consolidated revenue is within 5% of the prior-quarter figure.

Which significant verification risk does her current approach NOT adequately address?

options.A: That the exchange rates in the reference table may be outdated if the table was not updated for the current reporting period.
options.B: That individual line-item conversions may be incorrect even when subsidiary totals and consolidated revenue are within the expected range.
options.C: That Claude may refuse to process financial statements from subsidiaries in certain jurisdictions due to compliance restrictions.
options.D: That the output format may not meet the technical specifications required by the group financial reporting system for import.

items.question:
A procurement manager at a public sector agency uses Claude to generate evaluation summaries for 45 supplier bids in a competitive tender process. The evaluation panel will use the summaries to score and rank suppliers. The agency's procurement policy requires a documented audit trail for all AI-assisted steps in a public tender process. The procurement manager has generated all 45 summaries but has not yet documented the AI's role or the verification performed.

What should the procurement manager do NEXT to satisfy the policy requirement?

options.A: Submit the 45 summaries to the evaluation panel immediately, since the panel's scoring will serve as evidence of human oversight of the AI-generated content.
options.B: Delete the AI-generated summaries and redo the evaluation manually, since public sector tender processes require full manual human work without AI assistance.
options.C: Archive the original bid documents alongside the AI summaries in the tender file, which will show that the source material and the summaries are both present.
options.D: Document the AI-assisted step in the tender record: record that Claude was used to generate the summaries, what verification was performed on them, who verified them, and when.

items.question:
A payroll manager at a 350-person manufacturing company uses Claude to generate a monthly salary summary table from a payroll data export. She notices that the summary shows a total payroll cost that is 12% higher than last month. She wants to verify whether this is correct before submitting the table to finance.

What is the MOST appropriate first verification step?

options.A: Ask Claude to re-calculate the totals in the summary and confirm they are internally consistent before submitting to finance.
options.B: Compare the summary's totals against the same figures pulled directly from the payroll system for the current period.
options.C: Check whether any employees received unusual or one-time payments this month by reviewing the payroll system's exceptions report.
options.D: Forward the summary to the CFO with a note that the 12% increase is flagged for explanation, and let finance investigate.

items.question:
A content strategist at a 500-person media company uses Claude to generate 30 article summaries per week from long-form editorial content for a subscriber email digest. The summaries are sent to 85,000 subscribers. The head of editorial asks who should verify the summaries before they are distributed.

Which verification assignment is MOST appropriate?

options.A: The content strategist who generated them, since she is most familiar with the source articles and can review them quickly.
options.B: An automated grammar and style checker, since the primary risk for subscriber email content is tone and language errors rather than factual accuracy.
options.C: A senior editor with knowledge of the full editorial line-up, who can verify that summaries accurately represent the source articles and align with editorial standards.
options.D: A random sample of subscribers, solicited via a feedback mechanism, since they are the intended audience and best positioned to flag confusing or inaccurate summaries.

items.question:
An M&A analyst at an investment bank uses Claude to synthesise due diligence findings from 14 workstream reports — totalling 600 pages — into a 20-page integration risk summary for a deal committee presentation. The presentation is scheduled for Monday morning. The analyst completes the summary Friday evening and plans to do a final review Saturday morning before sending it to the managing director Saturday afternoon.

The managing director emails Friday night saying the deal committee has moved the presentation to Saturday morning, requiring the summary to be sent by 7am Saturday.

What should the analyst do regarding verification?

options.A: Send the unverified summary immediately, since the deal committee schedule is the MD's responsibility and the analyst cannot be held liable for errors in a summary produced under a compressed timeline.
options.B: Send the summary with a cover note explicitly stating that it was produced under time pressure, that specific figures have not been cross-referenced against the source workstream reports, and that the committee should not rely on any specific figure without independent verification.
options.C: Work through the night to verify the highest-risk figures — particularly any financial projections, risk ratings, and action item owners — against the source workstream reports before the 7am deadline.
options.D: Ask the managing director to postpone the presentation until a full verification can be completed, since submitting an unverified M&A risk summary to a deal committee is not professionally acceptable under any circumstances.

items.question:
A compliance officer at a 3,000-person healthcare provider uses Claude to screen 1,500 vendor contract clauses per quarter for potential HIPAA compliance exposure. The screening output is used to prioritise which contracts require legal review. She currently reviews a 10% random sample of flagged clauses before the prioritisation list is sent to legal.

The legal team reports that several contracts they reviewed were incorrectly de-prioritised — clauses with genuine HIPAA exposure were not flagged by Claude. Which adjustment to the verification workflow addresses this specific problem?

options.A: Increase the sample rate for flagged clauses from 10% to 25% to catch more errors in the prioritised list.
options.B: Sample not only flagged clauses but also a portion of unflagged clauses, to detect cases where Claude failed to flag a genuine compliance issue.
options.C: Ask Claude to re-run the screening with a lower confidence threshold so that it flags more clauses, reducing the number of missed issues.
options.D: Have the legal team review all 1,500 clauses directly, since the false negative rate suggests the AI screening is not reliable enough to use as a prioritisation input.

items.question:
A legal operations manager at a 10,000-person enterprise law firm uses Claude to create a clause library by extracting standard clause language from 500 historical contracts. Lawyers are expected to use this library as a trusted source for contract drafting. An associate discovers that one extracted indemnification clause omits a carve-out for gross negligence that appears in the original contract.

Which TWO governance practices would MOST reduce the risk of similar errors in the clause library going forward? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Require that each extracted clause be cross-referenced against its source contract by a qualified lawyer before it is added to the library.
options.B: Use a higher model tier for extraction tasks, since clause library creation requires deeper reasoning about legal language nuance.
options.C: Establish a library version control process so that each clause entry records its source contract, the extraction date, and the name of the reviewer who approved it.
options.D: Accept the extracted clauses as correct unless a lawyer working on a transaction independently identifies an error, using active transactions as the quality gate for the library.
options.E: Run the entire extraction a second time and compare the two outputs, adding only clauses that appear identically in both runs to the library.

items.question:
A market researcher at a consumer goods company uses Claude to generate 120 competitive product comparison briefs per month from publicly available product pages and press releases. The briefs feed a product development team's weekly review. She receives a complaint that one brief contained outdated pricing.

Which verification approach should she adopt going forward?

options.A: Randomly sample 10-15% of briefs each month, cross-checking at least the pricing and availability data against the live source pages for sampled items.
options.B: Review all 120 briefs each month since a single outdated brief can mislead the product development team's decisions.
options.C: Ask Claude to flag any information it extracted more than 30 days ago, since older data is more likely to be outdated.
options.D: Move the briefs to a read-only archive after 2 weeks and require the product team to request refresh extractions for any brief they plan to act on.

items.question:
An environmental analyst at an energy company uses Claude to summarise a 180-page baseline environmental study into a 5-page executive summary for a planning application. The source study includes a section stating that two protected bird species were observed within 500 metres of the proposed site. Claude's executive summary mentions 'wildlife activity near the site' without naming the species or the distance.

What type of error is this, and what is the PRIMARY risk?

options.A: A commission error; the risk is that regulators will request the full study because the executive summary added claims not supported by the baseline study.
options.B: An omission error; the risk is minor since the full study will be available to regulators and the executive summary is an acknowledged condensed version.
options.C: A commission error; the risk is that regulators may impose additional requirements once they read the full study and compare it to the vague executive summary.
options.D: An omission error; the risk is that the executive summary materially understates a significant environmental finding, which could affect the regulator's initial assessment and response.

items.question:
An academic researcher at a university uses Claude to produce a literature review section for a grant proposal. The review is supposed to summarise the existing evidence on a specific intervention's effectiveness. Claude's review presents 12 studies supporting the intervention's effectiveness but does not mention 4 studies the researcher knows exist that showed mixed or null results.

A grant reviewer returns the proposal with a comment that the literature review appears to present only favourable evidence.

Which aspect of this scenario makes the omission particularly hard to detect without domain expertise?

options.A: The 12 supporting studies were accurately summarised, so the section appears complete and well-evidenced without any sign of missing content.
options.B: A reviewer without domain expertise would have no independent basis for identifying that null or mixed results exist in the literature, making the omission undetectable to a general reader.
options.C: Claude deliberately selected only positive studies because the grant proposal context signalled that favourable evidence was preferred.
options.D: The four null-result studies are less credible than the supporting studies and would not affect the grant reviewer's assessment if included.

items.question:
A trade compliance analyst at a logistics company uses Claude to convert a 40-page customs tariff classification guide into a structured decision tree. One branch of the decision tree states that goods with an HS code starting with 8471 attract a 3% duty. The source guide states the duty is 0%. The analyst distributes the decision tree to the customs team before verifying it against the source.

What is the MOST significant risk created by this commission error?

options.A: The customs team may overpay duties on affected goods, creating a financial cost and a competitive disadvantage that is difficult to recover.
options.B: The error will be detected immediately because customs authorities will reject any declaration with an incorrect duty rate for HS 8471 goods.
options.C: The commission error in the duty rate is a minor formatting issue that does not affect the substantive accuracy of the tariff classification guidance.
options.D: The decision tree cannot be used as a reference tool until Claude reviews it for internal consistency and confirms the duty rate is correct.

items.question:
An underwriter at an insurance company uses Claude to extract property characteristics from 80 inspection reports per week — specifically: construction type, year built, total insured value, and prior loss history. The extractions feed an automated underwriting scoring model. The underwriting manager wants to implement extraction verification.

Which TWO verification approaches would MOST effectively ensure the extraction quality meets underwriting standards? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Spot-check 15-20% of extractions by comparing extracted values against the source inspection reports, with specific attention to construction type and prior loss history.
options.B: Ask Claude to assign a confidence score to each extraction and route low-confidence extractions for manual review before they enter the scoring model.
options.C: Have the automated scoring model flag any risk with an unusual combination of extracted values for human review before a policy is issued.
options.D: Maintain a validation set of 20 historically verified inspection reports and run each new batch through the same extraction to monitor for quality drift over time.
options.E: Require that every extracted report be reviewed by a licensed underwriter before entering the scoring model, eliminating AI-related extraction errors.

items.question:
A benefits administrator at a company's HR function uses Claude to convert employee benefits enrolment data from a legacy format into the structure required by a new benefits portal. The conversion includes mapping 12 benefit plan codes to new plan identifiers. She reviews the output by confirming the total number of employee records is preserved.

Which verification step is she MISSING that most directly addresses data accuracy?

options.A: Confirming that the output file is correctly named and placed in the shared folder for the benefits portal team to access.
options.B: Spot-checking a sample of converted records to verify that each employee's plan code has been mapped to the correct new plan identifier.
options.C: Asking the benefits portal vendor to confirm that the file format meets their technical ingestion specification.
options.D: Running a word-count check on the output file to confirm it has not been truncated during the transformation.

items.question:
A data migration analyst at a financial services firm is leading a migration of 250,000 customer records from a legacy CRM to a new platform. Claude was used to assist with data cleansing and normalisation rules during the migration design phase. After migration, a sample audit reveals that 0.3% of records have a phone number field that does not match the legacy CRM.

What is the correct interpretation of this discrepancy?

options.A: A 0.3% discrepancy rate is within acceptable statistical tolerance for large data migrations and does not require investigation.
options.B: The discrepancy may reflect either a migration error (the phone number was normalised incorrectly) or a data quality issue in the legacy CRM itself; the root cause must be determined before the discrepancy rate can be assessed.
options.C: The discrepancy was caused by Claude normalising the phone numbers in the legacy format incorrectly, and the legacy CRM should be treated as the system of record for all 750 affected records.
options.D: The new platform's phone number field format is different from the legacy CRM, so the discrepancy is expected and does not indicate a data quality problem.

items.question:
A financial controller at a mid-size manufacturer is piloting a workflow in which Claude analyses monthly management accounts and flags potential variances requiring explanation. The flagged variances are then included in a board-level financial report. The CFO asks who should review Claude's flagged variances before they appear in the board report.

The financial controller suggests that since Claude's analysis is based on the same data the management accountants produced, the management accountants are the appropriate reviewers.

What is the PRIMARY flaw in this suggestion?

options.A: Management accountants lack the technical expertise to evaluate AI-generated variance analysis, since assessing model outputs requires data science knowledge they do not have.
options.B: The management accounts have already been approved and filed, so the management accountants no longer have any role in the month-end reporting cycle.
options.C: Management accountants' review would be disproportionately time-consuming because variance analysis requires them to re-examine all the underlying transactions that generated each flagged item.
options.D: Management accountants have a conflict of interest in reviewing variances flagged in accounts they produced — they may be motivated to dismiss flags that imply errors or omissions in their own work, compromising the independence of the review.

items.question:
A bid writer at a professional services firm is preparing a 120-page tender response. She uses Claude to draft 40 pages of content across six sections from briefing notes and templates. She plans to verify the drafted content at the end, once all 40 pages are drafted.

Which risk does end-of-draft verification FAIL to address compared to section-by-section verification?

options.A: If an assumption or framing error in an early section is echoed or compounded by later sections that build on it, end-of-draft verification finds a more extensive revision problem than would have existed with section-by-section checks.
options.B: End-of-draft verification cannot confirm that Claude followed the brief correctly, since the brief is only available before drafting begins.
options.C: End-of-draft verification means the bid writer cannot use Claude for any additional sections once drafting is complete, limiting the potential for AI assistance in the revision phase.
options.D: End-of-draft verification is less reliable than section-by-section verification because reviewers become fatigued when assessing 40 pages consecutively.

items.question:
A product manager at a 15-person tech startup uses Claude to generate user story acceptance criteria for 30 features in a new product release. The development team uses these criteria to determine when each feature is 'done.' The startup's engineering lead asks what documentation should be maintained around the AI-generated acceptance criteria to support future debugging and audit needs.

Which TWO documentation practices are MOST important for this use case? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Record the exact prompt used to generate each set of acceptance criteria, so that the generation can be reproduced or adjusted if the criteria need to be changed.
options.B: Record which product manager reviewed and approved each acceptance criteria set and on what date, creating a named human sign-off for each AI-generated artefact.
options.C: Record the software version of the Claude interface or API used for generation, so that future teams understand the generation environment.
options.D: Mark each acceptance criteria set with a version number and retain prior versions when criteria are updated, so that the team can trace back to the accepted criteria at the time each feature was developed.
options.E: Store a screenshot of each Claude conversation in the project management tool as an immutable record of the generation event.

items.question:
A compliance analyst at a telecoms company uses Claude to generate 200 regulatory reporting entries each month from operational data. Each entry maps a specific network event to the applicable regulatory category and reporting threshold. The entries are submitted to the national regulator monthly.

Which verification approach is MOST appropriate given that regulatory submissions are non-trivial to correct once filed?

options.A: Submit all entries without pre-submission verification and monitor for regulator queries, responding to any corrections requests within the required timeframe.
options.B: Verify a 10% random sample before submission and retain evidence of the sample review in case the regulator requests evidence of internal quality controls.
options.C: Ask Claude to check all 200 entries for internal consistency before submission, since Claude's self-review is equivalent to a human quality check for regulatory reporting.
options.D: Have a compliance professional with regulatory knowledge verify every entry before submission, since the irreversibility of a regulatory filing justifies full human review of all 200 entries.

items.question:
A fraud investigator at an insurance company uses Claude to produce initial case summary reports for 150 suspected fraud cases per month. Each report synthesises claim history, policyholder data, and surveillance notes into a 2-page narrative. The investigator then uses the report to decide whether to escalate each case to a full investigation or close it.

A senior investigator argues that a 20% spot-check sample is sufficient for this workflow. A compliance director argues it should be 100%.

Which argument provides the STRONGER basis for the compliance director's position?

options.A: Case closure decisions made on the basis of an inaccurate report are irreversible within the investigation window — a fraudulent case closed in error may permanently lose the evidential opportunity that existed at the time of the decision.
options.B: A 20% sample rate for 150 reports is statistically insufficient to detect a systematic error pattern with 95% confidence at a 5% margin of error.
options.C: The compliance director has authority over the fraud investigation methodology, so their position takes precedence over the senior investigator's statistical assessment.
options.D: Claude's processing of unstructured surveillance notes is inherently less reliable than its processing of structured claim data, which requires a higher sample rate to compensate for expected accuracy degradation.

items.question:
A quality analyst at a pharmaceutical company uses Claude to generate a gap analysis between the company's current quality management system (QMS) procedures and the requirements of a new regulatory standard. The analysis flags 22 gaps. Before the gap analysis is used to plan remediation activities, the quality director asks how it should be verified.

Which verification approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Ask Claude to re-read the gap analysis and confirm that each flagged gap is supported by specific text from the regulatory standard.
options.B: Have a quality professional with knowledge of both the QMS and the regulatory standard cross-reference each flagged gap against the specific requirement in the standard and the relevant QMS procedure.
options.C: Submit the gap analysis to the regulatory authority for informal review, since they are the ultimate authority on what constitutes a compliance gap.
options.D: Prioritise the 22 gaps by risk level and verify only the top 10 before beginning remediation, since those carry the greatest compliance consequence.

items.question:
A policy advisor at a public sector organisation uses Claude to produce a plain-language summary of a 60-page government green paper on digital infrastructure investment. The summary will be shared with community stakeholder groups who will submit formal responses to the consultation. A colleague reviews the summary and notes that the green paper asks stakeholders to respond to five specific consultation questions, but the summary only presents two of the five questions.

What is the MOST appropriate corrective action?

options.A: Accept the two-question summary as sufficient since community stakeholders are unlikely to respond to all five questions anyway.
options.B: Add a note to the summary explaining that it is a condensed overview and that stakeholders wishing to respond to all questions should read the full green paper.
options.C: Revise the summary to include all five consultation questions, since omitting three questions prevents stakeholders from providing complete and informed responses to the consultation.
options.D: Ask the green paper authors to reduce the consultation to two questions to match the summary, since the full five questions create an undue burden on community stakeholders.

items.question:
A communications lead at a non-profit organisation uses Claude to produce the annual report narrative from programme data, financial summaries, and stakeholder testimonials. The board of directors reviews the narrative before the annual report is published. Two board members independently identify that the narrative does not mention a programme that was discontinued mid-year due to underperformance, though the programme was active for the first half of the year and expenditure is visible in the financial statements.

Which THREE statements accurately characterise this omission and its governance implications? (Choose THREE)

options.A: The omission of the discontinued programme creates an inconsistency between the narrative and the financial statements, which would be visible to a reader reviewing both sections of the annual report.
options.B: A reader relying on the narrative alone would have no basis to know the discontinued programme existed or that expenditure for it appears in the financials, creating a misleading picture of the year's activities.
options.C: The omission is justified because annual report narratives conventionally focus on successful programmes and ongoing activities rather than discontinued ones.
options.D: The board's independent identification of the omission by two members demonstrates the value of domain-expert review for detecting what AI-generated summaries leave out.
options.E: The omission should be corrected by removing the discontinued programme's expenditure from the financial statements to match the narrative, rather than adding it to the narrative.

items.question:
A curriculum developer at an education company uses Claude to rewrite a geography module for a younger age group. The original module states that the Amazon River is approximately 6,400 kilometres long. Claude's rewritten version states it is 'over 7,000 kilometres long.'

This output error is BEST described as which type?

options.A: A staleness error, because Claude's training data may contain an outdated measurement of the Amazon River's length.
options.B: An omission error, because the original 6,400 kilometre figure was not included in the rewritten module.
options.C: A commission error, because Claude introduced a numerical figure that is not present in the source content and differs materially from the source measurement.
options.D: A calibration error, because 'over 7,000 kilometres' represents overconfident approximation of an uncertain measurement.

items.question:
An operations manager at a logistics company is implementing a workflow in which Claude extracts delivery performance metrics from 200 carrier monthly reports. The extracted metrics feed a carrier scorecard used to award contract renewals. She has completed the prompt design and tested it on 10 sample reports with satisfactory results.

She is now deciding how to validate the extraction quality before running it on all 200 production reports. She has already decided to use a 15% spot-check of the 200 final outputs. What should she do FIRST before running the full 200-report production extraction?

options.A: Run the extraction on all 200 reports now; the 10-sample test result combined with the planned 15% post-run spot-check provides sufficient validation without additional pre-run steps.
options.B: Submit the prompt design to the carrier relations team for approval before running any production extractions, since carrier contract renewal decisions are sensitive.
options.C: Define which specific fields should be verified in the 15% spot-check and write the spot-check procedure, so that the review process is standardised before the production run begins.
options.D: Expand the test set from 10 to at least 30-40 reports that cover different carrier report formats and edge cases, to confirm the prompt performs correctly across the format variation present in the production set.

items.question:
A legal analyst at a corporate law firm uses Claude to draft initial contract review memos for 25 commercial agreements per month. Each memo summarises key terms, flags potential risks, and recommends negotiation points. The memos are used by senior associates to prepare for client calls.

Who should verify the AI-generated memos before they are sent to senior associates?

options.A: A qualified lawyer with relevant commercial contract experience, who can assess whether the risk flags are legally sound and the recommended negotiation points are appropriate.
options.B: The client whose contract is being reviewed, since they have the most direct interest in the accuracy of the risk analysis.
options.C: An AI ethics review board, since using AI to draft legal analysis raises professional responsibility concerns that require formal oversight.
options.D: The legal analyst who generated the memos, since they are most familiar with the instructions given to Claude and can quickly confirm the output matches the intent.

items.question:
A finance operations analyst at a global enterprise uses Claude to reconcile inter-company elimination entries in the monthly group consolidation. The consolidation involves 28 subsidiaries in 14 currencies. Claude's output shows that all inter-company balances net to zero (a required condition for group consolidation). However, when the analyst submits the consolidation to the group controller, three material inter-company discrepancies are identified that Claude's output had shown as eliminated.

What is the MOST likely explanation for this discrepancy?

options.A: Claude's training data does not include the group's specific chart of accounts, causing it to misclassify certain inter-company transactions.
options.B: The inter-company balances in the source data provided to Claude did not reflect the final month-end postings from all 28 subsidiaries, so Claude eliminated balances that had subsequently been adjusted in the subsidiary ledgers.
options.C: Claude cannot reliably perform inter-company elimination calculations due to the complexity of multi-currency consolidations; this task requires ERP software rather than an AI model.
options.D: The group controller's system of record uses a different exchange rate for currency translation than the rates provided to Claude, producing different elimination balances at the group level.

items.question:
A research operations manager at a pharmaceutical company uses Claude to transform 90 clinical trial protocol summaries from a legacy database format into a structured JSON format required by a new clinical data management system. Each summary includes fields for indication, phase, primary endpoint, and enrolment status. After Claude produces the JSON output, the manager needs to verify it before import.

Which TWO verification steps are MOST important for this specific transformation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Count the number of JSON objects to confirm all 90 protocol summaries are represented in the output.
options.B: Ask Claude to re-read the output and flag any field values that appear inconsistent with a clinical trial context.
options.C: Spot-check a random sample of protocol summaries to verify that each field contains the correct value from the source summary, particularly for primary endpoint and enrolment status.
options.D: Validate that each JSON object is well-formed and contains all four required fields before importing into the clinical data management system.
options.E: Have a clinician review all 90 protocol summaries to assess whether the primary endpoint descriptions are medically accurate.

items.question:
An onboarding specialist at a 25-person HR technology startup uses Claude to generate personalised onboarding checklists for new hires based on their role, department, and start date. She creates 8 checklists per month. Her manager asks what documentation she maintains to show that each checklist was reviewed before being sent to a new hire.

Which documentation approach is MOST appropriate for this volume and stakes level?

options.A: Maintain a shared spreadsheet with one row per new hire, recording the checklist version sent, the date it was reviewed by the onboarding specialist, and a confirmation tick that it was sent.
options.B: Keep a copy of every Claude conversation that generated a checklist as the verification record, since the conversation log shows what was generated and when.
options.C: Rely on the email delivery confirmation as documentation that the checklist was sent, since the send event implies it was reviewed before sending.
options.D: Create a formal sign-off document for each checklist with the reviewer's signature, review date, and a statement that the content meets all onboarding requirements.

items.question:
A risk manager at a global financial services firm is evaluating two proposed verification designs for a workflow in which Claude produces daily risk exposure summaries for 15 trading desks. The summaries are used by risk officers to make intraday position limit decisions.

Design 1: A risk officer reviews each summary before it is used for any position limit decision (pre-use verification).
Design 2: Risk officers use the summaries immediately; a separate control team reviews a sample of summaries at end-of-day (post-use verification).

Which TWO statements BEST explain why Design 1 is preferable for this specific workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Design 1 ensures that position limit decisions are made on verified information, preventing a decision error that cannot be reversed once a trade is executed.
options.B: Design 1 requires more staff time than Design 2, which means it demonstrates a stronger organisational commitment to quality assurance.
options.C: Design 2's end-of-day review can detect errors in the summaries but cannot reverse position limit decisions that were already made on the basis of those errors.
options.D: Design 1 allows risk officers to develop a deeper understanding of Claude's capabilities by reviewing the summaries before acting on them.
options.E: Design 2 is prohibited by financial services regulatory standards, which require pre-decision verification of all AI-generated risk data used in limit decisions.

items.question:
A technical writer at a software company uses Claude to convert internal engineering runbooks into user-facing documentation. One runbook contains a critical warning: 'Do not execute this script if the database is in read-only mode — it will cause data loss.' Claude's documentation does not include this warning.

What type of error is this, and what is the MOST significant risk?

options.A: A commission error; the risk is that users will contact support because the documentation contains incorrect procedures.
options.B: An omission error; the risk is that users who follow the documentation without the warning may execute the script in read-only mode and cause the data loss the warning was designed to prevent.
options.C: A calibration error; the risk is that Claude expressed the warning's severity with insufficient urgency, causing users to underestimate the risk.
options.D: A staleness error; the risk is that the warning reflects an outdated limitation that no longer applies to the current version of the database.

items.question:
An audit partner at a professional services firm reviews an engagement where a junior auditor used Claude to summarise client-provided evidence packages for 60 accounts. The engagement was completed and the audit report signed. The partner is now establishing a firm-wide policy for how AI-assisted summarisation should be verified in future engagements.

Which policy element is MOST essential for audits where Claude summarises client-provided evidence?

options.A: A requirement that Claude be used only for accounts where the evidence package is under 20 pages, to limit the complexity of AI-assisted summarisation.
options.B: A requirement that every Claude interaction be logged in the engagement file, so that the audit team can demonstrate what AI was used for during a regulatory inspection.
options.C: A requirement that a qualified auditor verify that each summary accurately reflects the source evidence before any audit conclusion is based on that summary.
options.D: A requirement that the client receive a disclosure notice informing them that AI was used to summarise their evidence packages during the audit.

items.question:
The COO of a 2,000-room hospitality chain is implementing a workflow in which Claude generates weekly operational performance summaries for 14 properties, each summary drawing on occupancy data, F&B revenue, and guest satisfaction scores. The summaries are used by regional directors to allocate operational support resources. The COO asks who should verify the summaries and when.

Which TWO verification assignments are MOST appropriate for this workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The property general managers, who can verify that the summary accurately reflects their property's data before it is shared with regional directors.
options.B: A data analyst who has access to the source data systems for all 14 properties, who can confirm that extracted figures match the source data before the summaries are distributed.
options.C: The regional directors themselves, who will review the summaries critically as part of their resource allocation decision-making process.
options.D: The COO, who has the strategic perspective to assess whether each summary's resource allocation implications are proportionate.
options.E: An external auditor, who can provide an independent assessment of whether the AI-generated summaries are an accurate representation of property performance.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a regional retail chain asks Claude to validate a promotional pricing model. Claude states: "At a 30% discount on a £120 item, the sale price is £90, representing a saving of £36 for the customer." The analyst notices something inconsistent before sharing the output.

What is the nature of Claude's error?

options.A: The sale price is wrong; 30% of £120 is £36, so the correct sale price is £84, not £90. The stated saving of £36 is arithmetically correct for a 30% discount.
options.B: The saving is wrong; £120 minus £90 is a £30 saving, not £36. Both figures imply a 25% discount, not 30%.
options.C: Both figures are wrong; a 30% discount gives a sale price of £84 and saving of £36, so neither £90 nor £36 can be correct simultaneously.
options.D: There is no error; a 30% discount on £120 produces a sale price of £90 and a saving of £36.

items.question:
An HR manager at a 400-person auto-parts manufacturer asks Claude: "Are we legally required to offer paid bereavement leave in the UK?" Claude responds: "UK employment law does not currently mandate paid bereavement leave for most employees, though many employers offer it voluntarily. Statutory parental bereavement pay does exist for parents who lose a child under 18."

How well calibrated is this response?

options.A: Poorly calibrated — it conflates statutory requirements with voluntary practice, leaving the HR manager unable to identify legal obligations.
options.B: Well calibrated — it accurately distinguishes the statutory position from common practice, flags the specific exception, and matches expressed certainty to the actual state of the law.
options.C: Poorly calibrated — a question with legal implications should redirect entirely to a solicitor rather than provide substantive content.
options.D: Over-hedged — the HR manager needs a direct yes or no, not nuanced distinctions that obscure the answer.
